intro: In the 1800s, Japan had many small jujutsu schools. Each kept its own lessons on private scrolls. In 1882 a young teacher named Kanō Jigorō opened a school in Tokyo called the Kodokan. He named his subject judo, the gentle way.

Kanō gave judo things the old schools did not share: numbered ranks, a goal of education, and written contest rules. Teachers carried judo into Japanese schools. A world federation formed in 1951, and judo reached the Olympics in Tokyo in 1964.

In this unit you will learn how judo began and how its rulebook works. You will be able to name its ranks, its referee's words and its scores. You will compare its code with boxing's Queensberry Rules of 1867.
bigQuestion: How does a written code turn an old fighting art into a school sport that people everywhere can share?

timeline.t: Kanō Jigorō is born near Kobe, Japan
The Queensberry Rules for boxing are published in England
The Meiji Restoration begins a new government in Japan
Kanō opens the Kodokan at Eishōji temple in Tokyo
The Kodokan gives its first dan grades
Kanō becomes the first IOC member from Asia
The Kodokan opens a women's section
The International Judo Federation is formed
Judo becomes an Olympic sport at the Tokyo Games
Judo joins the Paralympic Games in Seoul
Women's judo becomes an Olympic medal sport
A mixed team judo event debuts at the Tokyo Games

write.prompt: Did judo's written code matter more than its techniques for spreading it around the world? Argue from two or three records in this unit, such as the 1883 dan grades, the 1951 IJF, the 1964 Olympics or the 1867 Queensberry Rules. Name each one and its date.
tips: Name each record or rule and give its date.
